patterns.usage_note: Colloquial contraction of goal-marking には, so it carries は's contrastive force: 店にゃ行かない sets that destination against others rather than simply naming it. It belongs to casual speech and to fiction dialogue that wants a rough or old-fashioned voice, and it is essentially never written in neutral prose, where には or plain に is used instead. Compare へ, which is the plain directional marker with no contrastive coloring at all. Distinguish the identically written experiencer にゃ (俺にゃ分からない), which marks the person a capacity rests with rather than a destination.

examples.ruby: あんな店[みせ]にゃ二度[にど]と行[い]かないと決[き]めた。
examples.english: I've decided I'm never setting foot in that place again.

examples.ruby: その話[はなし]は社長[しゃちょう]にゃ通[とお]してあるから大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]だ。
examples.english: Don't worry, that one I've already run past the boss at least.

examples.ruby: この荷物[にもつ]は本社[ほんしゃ]にゃ送[おく]らなくていいよ。
examples.english: This one you don't have to send to head office, at least.

patterns.usage_note: へ points at the direction or endpoint of movement and, by extension, at the person a message or thing is headed for. Where に pins down arrival at a goal, へ typically keeps the focus on the heading, which is why it sounds slightly softer and is the usual choice on envelopes and dedications (山田様へ). Unlike its class-mate にゃ it is fully neutral and at home in writing.

examples.ruby: 来週[らいしゅう]の月曜[げつよう]に大阪[おおさか]へ出張[しゅっちょう]します。
examples.english: I'm heading to Osaka on business next Monday.

examples.ruby: 子[こ]どもたちが公園[こうえん]へ駆[か]け出[だ]していった。
examples.english: The kids went tearing off toward the park.

examples.ruby: 新[あたら]しい住所[じゅうしょ]を旧友[きゅうゆう]へ葉書[はがき]で知[し]らせた。
examples.english: I sent an old friend a postcard with my new address.
